{{Short description|Sequence of rational numbers}}
{{refimprove|date=January 2017}}

In [[mathematics]], '''a Göbel sequence'''  is a sequence of [[rational number]]s defined by the [[recurrence relation]]
:<math>x_n = \frac{ x_0^2+x_1^2+\cdots+x_{n-1}^2}{n-1},\!\,</math>
with starting value
:<math>x_0 = x_1 = 1.</math>
Göbel's sequence starts with
: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 28, 154, 3520, 1551880, ... {{OEIS|id=A003504}}
The first non-integral value is ''x''<sub>44</sub>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Guy|first1=Richard K.|title=Unsolved Problems in Number Theory|date=1981|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=978-1-4757-1740-2|page=120}}</ref>

== History ==
This sequence was developed by the German mathematician [[Fritz Göbel]] in the 1970s.<ref name=":0" /> In 1975, the Dutch mathematician [[Hendrik Lenstra]] showed that the 44th term is not an integer.<ref name=":0" />

==Generalization==
Göbel's sequence can be generalized to ''k''th powers by
:<math>x_n = \frac{1+x_0^k+x_1^k+\cdots+x_{n-1}^k}{n},</math>
with starting value
:<math>x_0 = 1.</math>

The least indices at which the ''k''-Göbel sequences assume a non-integral value are
:43, 89, 97, 214, 19, 239, 37, 79, 83, 239, ... {{OEIS|id=A108394}}
Regardless of the value chosen for ''k'', the initial 19 terms are always integers.<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=2307.09741 |title=How Long Can ''k'' -Göbel Sequences Remain Integers? |date=2024|last1= Matsuhira|first1= Rinnosuke|last2= Matsusaka|first2= Toshiki|last3= Tsuchida|first3= Koki|journal= The American Mathematical Monthly|volume= 131|issue= 9|pages= 784–793|doi= 10.1080/00029890.2024.2379748}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Stone |first=Alex |date=2023 |title=The Astonishing Behavior of Recursive Sequences |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-astonishing-behavior-of-recursive-sequences-20231116/ |access-date=2023-11-17 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref>
